title: True Crime: The Roots of an American Obsession
author: Walter Mosley
citation: Mosley, Walter. 'True Crime: The Roots of an American Obsession.' Newsweek, 2009.

sections.heading: True Crime: The Roots of an American Obsession

epigraph.quote: We are fascinated by true crime because we are all guilty of something.

paragraphs: We are fascinated by true crime because we are all guilty of something. Even the most law-abiding citizen among us has harbored dark thoughts, petty resentments, or sudden flashes of violent rage. When we open a newspaper or watch a television documentary about a heinous murder, we are peering through a barred window into the dark basement of our collective human condition.

True crime stories offer us something that everyday life rarely provides: moral clarity and an ending. In reality, injustice often goes unpunished, questions linger without answers, and suffering seems entirely arbitrary. But in the structured narrative of a crime investigation, the transgressor is pursued, the evidence is gathered, and the law steps forward to re-establish order.

Yet there is a deeper, more troubling allure to these tales. By reading about the extreme deviations of killers and thieves, we reassure ourselves of our own normalcy. We think: 'I may be flawed, I may be selfish, but I am not that.' The criminal becomes our scapegoat, carrying our unacknowledged sins out into the wilderness while we watch safely from the comfort of our living rooms.

Furthermore, the American obsession with true crime reflects our national obsession with individuality and freedom. The criminal is the ultimate perversion of the rugged individualist—a person who decides that the rules governing the rest of society simply do not apply to them. In studying their downfall, we affirm the boundaries of the social contract while secretly marveling at the audacity of those who dare to break it.
